title: What Was Actually Agreed
subtitle: A pact witnessed by many and written by none
imageCaption: The festival was extensively observed and almost entirely unrecorded, which Waluigi suspects was arranged.
hook: Everyone present agrees a pact was made at the Festival of the Fallen. The other side did not need to agree: it had legislated years earlier and posted the notice three streets away.

background.why: Started as a Midlands mercenary company that decided it would rather be the client than serve one, and became a state. Motto: Order Through Compliance. Currently expanding its emergency authority — which is the legal instrument this file keeps colliding with.

Waluigi watched a Rakasha use the Midnight Portal at Ferngrove from behind a hedge, and concluded it was not a first visit — that the portal is a regular transit point for Rakasha movement, possibly commuting to Raventree business. Context for how the clans move without being on anyone's register.
Waluigi's unauthorized audit of which factions are genuinely strong and which are paper tigers with good marketing. Read it to judge what the rakasha thought they were buying, and what it was worth.

brief:
**The short version.** A pact was made at the Festival of the Fallen. Everyone present agrees on that. The problem is that only one side has ever written anything down.

The rakasha side recorded four lines in a memorandum while the words were being spoken. The Iron Legion side did not need to record anything that night, because it had passed the relevant law years earlier and nailed the notice up three streets from where the festival was held.

**This file set out to put the two accounts side by side and discovered there is no second account to put there.** What looks like an agreement between two parties is one party's ceremony and another party's paperwork, and the paperwork was written first.


Waluigi cannot deliver the two columns and is going to explain why, because the reason turned out to be the finding.

There is no second column. One side of this agreement recorded terms — a memorandum taken at the circle, in four clauses, while the words were still being spoken. The other side recorded nothing, because the other side did not need to. It had already written its terms years earlier, in a statute, and the statute was posted three streets from the festival ground.

You cannot place a pact beside a licence and call them two accounts of the same thing.

## What this file is arguing

Twelve exhibits, and the argument is that **the pact was never the mechanism**. The pact was the occasion. The mechanism was administrative, it was already in force, and every step of it is documented by people who thought they were doing routine work.

Follow it.

*Asked of us:* that armed men of the Loyalist establishment be quartered within the district, permanently, and at the district's own request. *Offered to us:* recognition, standing, the rite completed rather than abandoned. One voice objected — **a garrison you asked for is still a garrison** — and was answered: **a garrison you asked for is a garrison you can un-ask.**

The answer is the best sentence anybody said that night and it is false. Clause 7 of the Iron Mandate exempts men maintained at the request of a recognised authority where the request is recorded. Clause 9 provides that the Legion determines what is a recognised authority. The request is the door and the Legion holds the handle, and the memorandum's own last line records that nobody in the circle raised the Mandate at all.

Then the offering list, where the ceremony's four traditional offerings — grain, salt, oil, and a name from each household — are ruled off by the clerk, and a fifth entry appears **below the line in a second hand**: *an undertaking, given aloud, on behalf of the living.* No giver named.

And then the Supernatural Sovereignty Act, posted in that district, that quarter. The offence is complete on the giving; performance is not required; it is triable as sedition; and where the undertaking is given collectively, every person present who did not dissent aloud is taken to have given it.

One voice dissented aloud. Everybody else in that circle is, on the face of the notice, a seditionist — and the entry that carefully omitted the speaker's name protects nobody, because the Act does not require one.

## What actually happened afterwards

The quartering return is where the file stops being about a ceremony.

Thirty-six men, six premises. Twenty-four in the old customs shed and twelve in two riverside houses, compensation paid for both. And three more premises taken with no men in them and no compensation, entered as *not occupied* — a term the return itself defines as premises to which the garrison holds the key and in which no man sleeps.

The three empty buildings are the district meeting hall, the upper floor of the granary, and the east gatehouse that housed the district watch. Its capacity to gather, to eat, and to police itself.

The petition confirms that the district worked this out before the archive did. One hundred and forty-one signatures out of four hundred households; thirty-eight refusals, thirty-one of them giving the same reason — *the grain is in the granary and the garrison has the key.* Support strongest in the riverside streets where soldiers actually sleep in people's front rooms, weakest nearest the food.

And the Legion patrol book, twelve weeks, two columns on the same page. The Trade Ward holds flat at twenty-one or twenty-two every week. The district runs eighteen, nineteen, then falls to zero by week twelve, with a standing instruction entered in week nine: *district policed by arrangement. Patrols not required.*

The Legion did not move in after the pact. It **stopped coming**, and wrote down that an arrangement now did the work.

## The retrieval, and what it cost

The earlier sessions explain why nobody was in a position to negotiate.

A portage bill from Cheep-Cheep Falls: three loads down at two hundred and ten pounds, two loads back up at two hundred and forty-eight. Thirty-eight pounds of something joined the party at the bottom of a waterfall and has been entered nowhere else.

An ambush at Rogueport laid in four positions, one of them **behind the party on the approach**, all occupied for hours before anyone arrived — on a route chosen that morning and told to four people. The counterpart of the silence contract lists, in its schedule, *the identity of the person who requested the route in advance*. Requested. Not learned, not overheard.

And an expenditure note: held, one, not divisible; expended, Rogueport; replacement, blank. *A second is not a purchase and cannot be requisitioned. It would have to be asked for, which is a different transaction with a different price.*

A party that has spent its only irreplaceable asset arrives at a negotiating circle with nothing to refuse with. Waluigi does not allege that anybody planned that sequence and cannot prove it. Waluigi observes that the ambush killed nobody, took nothing, and set no pursuit — and that a fortnight later the district agreed to a garrison.

WAH.

threads.title: There is no second column, and that is the finding
threads.text:
One side recorded terms in a memorandum taken while they were being spoken. The other side had written its terms years earlier in a statute and posted them three streets from the festival ground. A pact and a licence are not two accounts of the same agreement, and the archive can no longer pretend the columns are commensurable.

**In plain terms:** there is no second version of this agreement, and that absence is the finding. One side made a promise; the other side had already written a law. A promise and a licence are not two accounts of one deal.

threads.title: Clause 7 is the door and clause 9 is the handle
threads.text:
The Iron Mandate exempts armed men maintained at the request of a recognised authority where the request is recorded — and lets the Legion determine what a recognised authority is. *A garrison you asked for is a garrison you can un-ask* was the best sentence spoken that night and it describes a right the district does not have.

**In plain terms:** clause 7 lets a garrison stay if a recognised authority asked for it, and clause 9 lets the Legion decide who counts as a recognised authority. So the invitation can be withdrawn at will — by them, not by you.

threads.title: Clause 5 makes the observance the evidence
threads.text:
The Sovereignty Act treats every person present at a collective undertaking who did not dissent aloud as having given it. Exactly one voice objected. In a meeting, silence is assent and the clause is ordinary; in a rite, silence is the form of participation, and the district's own custom becomes the proof against it.

**In plain terms:** at a meeting, saying nothing means you agree. At a funeral rite, saying nothing is how you take part. The law was written for the first situation and applied to the second, so observing the ceremony correctly is what makes you guilty.

threads.title: Three buildings with nobody in them
threads.text:
The meeting hall, the upper floor of the granary, and the east gatehouse — taken, uncompensated, entered as *not occupied*, which the quartering return itself defines as premises the garrison holds the key to and in which no man sleeps. Thirty-one households refused to sign the petition because the grain is in the granary and the garrison has the key.

**In plain terms:** three buildings were taken, nobody was paid, and the return calls them "not occupied" — which by its own definition means the garrison holds the keys and nobody sleeps there. They are not billets. They are the meeting hall, the food store and the gate.

threads.title: They arrived with nothing to refuse with
threads.text:
Held one, not divisible, expended at Rogueport, replacement column blank — and a remark noting that a second would have to be *asked for*, which is a different transaction with a different price. The ambush that forced the expenditure killed nobody, took nothing and set no pursuit. Waluigi cannot prove the sequence was designed and declines to pretend the outcome was accidental.

**In plain terms:** the one thing that could have been used as leverage was spent at Rogueport, and the replacement column is blank. They walked into the festival with nothing to bargain with, and the ambush that emptied their hands killed nobody and took nothing.

leads.title: Record both parties' understanding of the pact
leads.objective: Abandoned as framed. There is no second column: one party recorded a memorandum at the circle, the other had already legislated. Both instruments are now filed, side by side, as exhibits rather than as columns.
leads.why: Separately is the only way it works — but the exercise assumed two parties keeping two accounts of one agreement. They were not. Closing this lead with the reason recorded is more honest than leaving it open against a method the evidence has refuted.

leads.title: Establish what was retrieved at Rogueport and for whom
leads.objective: Identify the retrieved article, its current custody, and whether it discharges any part of the pact. The portage bill puts it at thirty-eight pounds; that is the only measurement anybody has.
leads.why: A retrieval performed under an unwritten agreement can be claimed afterwards as either a favour or a payment, and the difference is the whole alliance. The party's one irreplaceable asset was spent getting it out, and nobody has yet written down what *it* is.

leads.title: Obtain the recorded request itself
leads.objective: Clause 7 of the Iron Mandate exempts only men maintained at a request that is *recorded*. Get the record: its form, its date, its custodian and its text.
leads.why: The grand argument about recognition is unwinnable because clause 9 lets the Legion decide it. The narrow one is winnable. The quartering return lists six premises and the terms memorandum records a request for quartering only — nobody at the circle asked anybody to take the assembly hall, the granary and the gatehouse. A discrepancy between two documents is a fight the district can have; a constitutional question is not.

leads.title: Get the rent receipts for number 18, Trade Ward
leads.objective: Forty gold a quarter at the punitive rate for an undeclared trade, paid in full, never appealed, held by an unnamed agent. Buy the payment record from the rating office.
leads.why: The purple emblem above the door is paint and this archive does not file paint. The rating column is different: it records that somebody with money chose the expensive silence over the cheap lie, on the same street as an ambush that needed a base. A device tells you what a tenant wants passers-by to think. A payment record tells you where the money comes from, and money leaves a name eventually.

leads.title: Get the district put back in the patrol book
leads.objective: Have the week-nine standing instruction — *district policed by arrangement, patrols not required* — rescinded, so that the district reappears in the same book as every other ward.
leads.why: Legion patrols are unwelcome and they are also the mechanism by which a ward remains part of the city's ordinary machinery: the same rota, the same officers, the same book anybody can inspect. Twelve weeks of zeros beside a Trade Ward column that never moves is not an absence of policing. It is the district's name still printed with nothing written against it, and somebody would have to write a new instruction to bring it back.

exhibits.title: Portage Bill — Thirty-Eight Pounds Joined the Party at the Falls
exhibits.onRecord: The carriers' bill for the Cheep-Cheep Falls portage. Three loads down, rated at two hundred and ten pounds, nine gold. Two loads back up, rated at two hundred and forty-eight pounds, fourteen gold. [[roll:3|Fewer loads returned and they weighed thirty-eight pounds more|which is a net acquisition of thirty-eight pounds at the bottom of a waterfall, entered nowhere else in any account the archive holds. The carriers rate by weight and do not open loads, so the bill records the mass of something nobody has described.|loads get repacked and combined constantly on a portage; the weights are approximate and prove nothing.]]. The party queried the upstream rate and paid it.
exhibits.analysis:
## The most boring document in the file

Waluigi wants to begin by conceding that this is a haulage invoice for nine and then fourteen gold pieces, and that nobody was ever meant to read it.

That is precisely why it is the first exhibit. Every other account of the falls comes from participants, and participants describe events. The carriers described weight, because weight is what they charge for, and weight is the one property of the expedition nobody thought to manage.

Three loads down. Two loads up. Two hundred and ten pounds becoming two hundred and forty-eight.

The consolidation from three loads to two is unremarkable — people repack after a descent, especially a wet one. The archive is not building anything on the load count.

The mass is a different matter. Loads can be recombined; pounds cannot be invented. [[roll:4|Repacking cannot increase total weight|it can change how many bundles there are and nothing else. The carriers weighed the whole consignment at both ends because they charge by it, and the difference is thirty-eight pounds of matter that was not present at the top of the falls.|the two weighings were taken by different men with different scales at different times of day and the difference is well within tolerance.]]

## What thirty-eight pounds is

The archive is going to be dull about this on purpose, because the alternative is speculation and the file has enough of that in the later sessions.

Thirty-eight pounds is not a document, a key, a ring, or a message. Those weigh ounces. It is not a person, a body, or a large quantity of treasure. It is roughly a full pack, a substantial stone object, a strongbox, or a quantity of metal.

It is also, notably, **more than one person can carry inconspicuously** while climbing a waterfall path, which is presumably why it went on the carriers' account at all. Anything smaller would have gone into somebody's pack and never appeared in any record.

So the retrieval at Cheep-Cheep Falls retrieved a physical object of substantial mass, and the reason the archive knows this is that it was too heavy to hide from the people being paid by the pound. Waluigi files that as the whole finding of this exhibit and declines to guess further, except to note that [[roll:5|the upstream rate query is more revealing than the weight|somebody in the party looked at the bill, saw the higher charge, questioned it, and then paid it without amending the weight entry. They had the chance to argue the tonnage down and did not, because arguing would have meant discussing the contents.|querying a bill and then paying it is what everybody does with every bill everywhere.]].

## Why the invoice survives and the account does not

There is a general lesson here that this investigation will lean on four more times, and Waluigi would rather state it early than repeat it.

The party's own record of the falls is a story told afterwards by people who were tired. It is unverifiable, self-serving in the ordinary human way, and — critically — it is *about* things. It describes a plunge, a difficulty, an outcome.

The carriers' bill is about none of that. It is about pounds and gold, produced by men with no interest in the expedition, filed by a hire office that keeps its books because otherwise it does not get paid.

That indifference is what makes it evidence. Nobody constructs an alibi in a portage ledger, because nobody imagines a portage ledger will ever be read against them.

The archive's standing instruction to anyone working this arc: [[roll:6|when the participants will not tell you what happened, find whoever charged them for it|the carriers, the ward tenancy office, the offering table clerk and the patrol book have all told this file more than the participants have, and none of them were trying to. Commercial records are hostile witnesses that do not know they are testifying.|participants' accounts remain the primary source and administrative scraps are only ever corroborative.]]

exhibits.title: Ambush Return — One Position Was Behind Them Before They Passed It
exhibits.visual: FOUR POSITIONS · ONE BEHIND
exhibits.onRecord: Four positions, reconstructed from marks on the ground after the Rogueport ambush. Roofline north, two sets of scuffing and a displaced tile. Alley mouths east and west, standing marks of a depth indicating hours rather than minutes. And a fourth position behind the party, on the approach, [[roll:4|occupied before the party walked past it|which is the finding. You cannot take a position behind a target unless you know the route the target will take, and you cannot hold it for hours unless you knew that route hours in advance.|a rear position is what any competent ambush party takes once it hears people coming up the street.]]. The route through the ward was chosen that morning and communicated to four people.
exhibits.analysis:
## Ambushes have a geometry and the geometry has a timestamp

Waluigi is aware that the party remembers this as chaos. Reconstructions do not care what anybody remembers.

Three of the four positions are unremarkable in themselves. A roofline overlooking a street and two alley mouths are where you would put people if you had a general idea that trouble would happen somewhere in this quarter. Any patrol commander with a map could choose them.

The fourth position is not like the other three, and the difference is not tactical, it is **evidential**.

A position behind the target, on the approach, only functions if the target passes it and keeps going. That means it has to be occupied before the target arrives, and it has to be on the specific street the target will use. Get the street wrong and the rear position is four people standing in an empty alley while the fight happens elsewhere.

So the rear position is a statement of certainty. Somebody was sure enough about the route to spend bodies on it. And the standing marks are deep, which means [[roll:5|they were sure hours ahead, not minutes|the ground records a prolonged wait. A tip-off received shortly before the party set out would produce a hasty three-position ambush on the likeliest street. This is a patient four-position ambush on the correct one.|deep standing marks accumulate quickly in soft ground and cannot be read as a duration with any confidence.]].

## Four people knew

The route was chosen that morning and communicated to four people. Waluigi has that from the party's own account and has no reason to doubt it, because it is the sort of detail nobody invents.

The archive is not going to name any of the four. It is going to state what the reconstruction narrows.

The leak was not of the destination — the destination was obvious and known to many. It was of the **route**, which is a different and much smaller piece of information, and it was passed early enough for four positions to be walked, chosen and occupied.

That rules out a considerable amount. It rules out observation on the day, because observers would have produced a following ambush, not a preceding one. It rules out a general warning, because a general warning does not tell you which alley. It rules out the party being tracked from the falls, because a tracked party is engaged when convenient, not funnelled into prepared ground.

What it leaves is somebody who knew the route in the morning and got it to the Legion with time to spare. The silence contract filed later in this session concedes the same thing in writing, which is the only reason Waluigi is prepared to state it this flatly: [[roll:6|two independent documents agree that the route was known in advance|the ground says the positions were prepared, and the schedule of a contract nobody expected the archive to read lists 'the identity of the person who requested the route in advance' as a matter that may not be spoken of. Neither document was made for the other.|ground reconstruction and a contract schedule are describing different things and the file is forcing them together.]].

## What the ambush was for

The last point is the one that reframes the session, and it comes from what the ambush did *not* do.

It did not kill anybody. It did not take the thirty-eight pounds. It did not hold the party. The contact was broken and the party extracted, and the reconstruction shows no pursuit positions at all — nobody was placed to follow them out.

An ambush laid with four prepared positions and hours of patience, which then lets the target leave, was not laid to destroy the target.

Set that against the expenditure note filed alongside this exhibit: the Tiger summon, held once, not divisible, spent here, not replaceable on any terms the party can meet.

Waluigi's reading is that the ambush accomplished exactly what it was designed to accomplish. **It made them spend it.** A party carrying an irreplaceable one-use asset into a negotiation is a party with an argument in reserve; a party that has already burned it arrives at the festival with nothing to spend, which is where the next session finds them.

The archive cannot prove intent and says so plainly. It can observe that the outcome was perfectly calibrated, and that [[roll:4|an ambush that costs the enemy their last card and takes no prisoners is a very cheap way to win a negotiation|four positions and no casualties on either side, in exchange for the other party arriving at the circle with an empty reserve. Whoever laid it either understood what the party was carrying or got extraordinarily lucky.|reading intent backwards from a favourable outcome is exactly the kind of reasoning this archive is supposed to refuse.]]

exhibits.title: Tenancy Schedule — Forty Gold a Quarter Not to Say What You Do
exhibits.onRecord: Five tenancies on one Trade Ward street. A chandler at six gold a quarter, a factor at eleven, a ropewalk at seven, a victualler at nine — and number 18, held by an agent, no name entered, no declared trade, paying forty. The ward rates undeclared tenancies punitively. [[roll:3|Number 18 pays the punitive rate quarterly, in full, and has never appealed|a tenant who thought the rating was unfair would appeal, because appeals are free and the sum is four times the street's average. Paying without complaint means the silence is worth more than thirty-one gold a quarter.|a wealthy tenant simply does not bother contesting a small municipal charge.]]. Above the door there is a device in purple. The ward does not register devices.
exhibits.analysis:
## The emblem is not the evidence

Waluigi is going to disappoint everybody immediately. The purple emblem above the door of number 18 is worthless as evidence and the file should stop citing it.

Devices are not registered by the ward. Anybody may hang anything above a door. The party saw a purple emblem and drew a conclusion, and the conclusion may well be right, but a painted board is not a document and this archive does not file paint.

What it files is the tenancy schedule, which is kept for rating purposes by clerks who have never heard of any of this, and which contains something a great deal harder to arrange than a sign.

Four tenants on this street declared a trade. Candles and oils. Grain brokerage. Cordage. Provisions. Each of them pays between six and eleven gold a quarter, because declared trades are rated on their trade.

Number 18 declared nothing, is held by an agent with no name entered, and pays forty. [[roll:4|The punitive rate is a price list for anonymity and somebody is buying at full retail|the ward does not care what you do, only that you write it down, and it charges roughly four times the going rate if you will not. Number 18 has decided that is a fair price, every quarter, indefinitely.|an agent-held tenancy with no declared trade is the ordinary arrangement for any absentee owner and the higher rate is a routine administrative default.]]

## What the rate rules out

The archive likes this document because it eliminates the boring explanations rather than confirming the exciting one.

It is not a vacant property. Vacant premises are rated differently and appear in a different column; number 18 is occupied and rated as occupied.

It is not a poor tenant hiding from a trade tax. Forty gold a quarter is far more than any of the declared trades on the street pay in rating, so the anonymity is costing more than the disclosure would.

It is not an oversight. An oversight gets corrected at the first quarter's demand, when somebody in an office writes a letter asking what you do. This has been paid repeatedly.

And it is not a dispute, because the ward's appeal process exists, is free, and has not been used.

So the field narrows to bodies that have money, want a fixed address in a commercial ward, and will pay a standing premium rather than enter a description of themselves in a public book. That is a short list of kinds of organisation, and [[roll:5|the rating column is doing the work the emblem cannot|a device above a door tells you what somebody wants passers-by to think. A rating entry tells you what they were willing to pay a municipal office to avoid writing down, which is a much more expensive and therefore much more sincere statement.|both are equally circumstantial and the file is dressing up an inference as a finding.]].

## Location, and the reason this sits in the ambush session

Waluigi filed this exhibit next to the ambush reconstruction deliberately and owes the reader the reason.

The reconstruction establishes that the route through the Trade Ward was known hours in advance and that four positions were prepared along it. A prepared ambush needs somewhere to prepare from — somewhere in the ward to gather, wait, and disperse to, which is not a rooftop or an alley mouth.

Number 18 is a premises in the Trade Ward, held by nobody in particular, doing nothing in particular, at a price that guarantees no clerk will ever ask a question about it.

The archive is explicitly not alleging that the ambush came out of number 18. It has no document connecting them, and manufacturing one would be exactly the failure this file criticises elsewhere.

What it records is the shape of the gap: an ambush that required a base, and a building on the same route whose entire expenditure profile is dedicated to not being asked what it is for. [[roll:6|The correct next step is the rent, not the door|forty gold a quarter is paid by somebody, through an agent, and the ward office holds the receipts. Money leaves a name eventually, and a rating clerk will produce a payment record for a fee where nobody will produce anything for a knock on the door.|the payment record will simply show the agent again and lead precisely nowhere.]]

exhibits.title: Expenditure Note — Expended, Replacement Column Blank
exhibits.secured: Expenditure note against the retrieval account
exhibits.onRecord: An expenditure note for a non-material asset. Held: one, not divisible. Expended: Rogueport, at the ambush. Effect: contact broken, party extracted. Replacement: dash. The remark attached: [[roll:5|"It was given once and the giving was a favour. A second is not a purchase and cannot be requisitioned. It would have to be asked for, which is a different transaction with a different price."|whoever wrote that understood the asset better than the people who spent it. A favour cannot be restocked; asking again converts a gift into a debt, and the price of the second is set by the giver, not the market.|standard quartermaster's language for anything that has to be sourced outside normal supply.]]. The retrieval succeeded. The reserve is nil.
exhibits.analysis:
## Filing a moment as a stores problem

Waluigi is aware that this is the exhibit that will annoy people, because the Tiger at Rogueport is the part of this arc anybody would want to tell a story about, and the archive has reduced it to a line item with a blank column.

That is deliberate and the archive will defend it.

A story about the Tiger tells you how it felt. An expenditure note tells you what the party has left, and what the party has left is what determines everything that happens at the festival two weeks later.

The note is precise in a way the story is not. **Held: one. Not divisible.** That second phrase is the important one, and it is doing more work than the first. Not divisible means it could not be spent partially, held in reserve, or split between two crises. It was a single indivisible use, which makes the decision to spend it a decision to have nothing.

And the effect column is honest about what it bought: contact broken, party extracted. Not victory. Not the destruction of the ambush. **Extraction.** [[roll:4|They spent an irreplaceable asset to leave a place|which is a legitimate use and may well have been the only one available, but it should be recorded as what it is. The account is one entry poorer and no objective was gained that was not already the objective before the ambush existed.|any expenditure that results in the party surviving is by definition a good expenditure and the framing here is unfair.]]

## The replacement column

The archive spends more time on blank fields than most readers think is reasonable, and this is the blank field that justifies the habit.

A quartermaster's note with an empty replacement column means one of two things. Either replacement is routine and nobody bothered to write *stores*, or replacement is impossible and there was nothing to write.

The remark settles it, and it settles it in unusually thoughtful language for a stores document. A second is not a purchase and cannot be requisitioned. It would have to be **asked for**, which is a different transaction with a different price.

Waluigi wants that distinction underlined because it is the entire economics of this investigation. A purchase has a market price known in advance and leaves both parties even. A request has a price set afterwards, by the party being asked, and leaves the asker owing.

The party's reserve therefore did not merely go to zero. It went to zero **with the only route to replenishment running through an obligation**, and the next session opens with the same party sitting in a circle being offered recognition in exchange for a garrison.

That sequence is not a coincidence in the conspiratorial sense; the archive is not claiming anybody planned it. It is a straightforward consequence, and [[roll:6|a party with nothing in reserve negotiates on the other side's terms as a matter of arithmetic, not character|they did not accept a bad price at the festival because they were foolish or frightened. They accepted it because the expenditure note two weeks earlier had already established that they had nothing left to refuse with.|the terms at the festival were driven by the ritual's demands and the party's reserves were irrelevant to them.]].

## What should have been entered

The archive will close with a criticism of the paperwork rather than of the people, which is its usual practice and also the more useful one.

This note was written after the fact. There is no corresponding entry from before — no record that the party ever accounted for holding a single indivisible irreplaceable asset while walking into a ward on a route four other people knew about.

Had that entry existed, the question *what happens if we have to spend it today* would have been on a page in front of somebody that morning.

That is not hindsight. It is the ordinary discipline of keeping a reserve register, which every quartermaster in every organisation in this archive's files maintains, and which this party does not.

Waluigi's recommendation for the arc going forward is procedural, unglamorous, and would have been worth more than the Tiger: keep the register. List what is held, what is divisible, what is replaceable and on what terms. Because [[roll:4|the party did not know it was carrying its only card until after it had played it|the remark about favours and prices was written in the past tense, afterwards, by somebody who had worked it out too late. Nobody in the ward that morning was operating on that understanding.|the party understood perfectly well what they had and made a considered choice under pressure.]]

exhibits.title: Silence Contract — Item Three Concedes There Is a Name
exhibits.secured: Counterpart copy with schedule attached and initialled
exhibits.visual: SCHEDULE · i ii iii iv
exhibits.onRecord: The counterpart of the silence contract, which unlike the famous copy has the schedule attached. The operative clause forbids communicating the scheduled matters to any person, without limit of time. The schedule lists four: the route taken through the Trade Ward; the number of persons informed of that route; [[roll:5|the identity of the person who requested the route in advance|which is the concession. A schedule of prohibited topics is a list of things that exist. Item iii states, in an executed instrument, that a specific identifiable person asked for the route before it was walked.|schedules are drafted broadly to cover hypotheticals and item iii need describe nobody real at all.]]; and any sum paid in connection with the first three. Consideration stated as received, amount not entered.
exhibits.analysis:
## Read the schedule, not the clause

Everybody in this arc can quote the operative clause. Waluigi has heard it recited three times and it says nothing: do not speak, write or by any sign communicate, to any person, without limit of time. That is boilerplate and appears in every silence contract ever drawn.

The schedule is where the drafting happened, and drafters are specific for a reason. Every item in a schedule costs money to negotiate and creates a risk if it is wrong, so nothing gets listed that does not need to be.

Item i: the route taken through the Trade Ward. So the route is a secret worth buying.

Item ii: the number of persons informed of that route. Not their names — the **number**. That is a strange thing to protect until you notice that a small number incriminates by itself.

Item iii: the identity of the person who requested the route in advance.

Item iv: any sum paid in connection with items i to iii.

Read as a set, that is not four unrelated prohibitions. It is a narrative in list form, and [[roll:4|the four items in sequence describe a transaction|a route existed, a limited number of people were told it, one of those people asked for it in advance, and money changed hands. The schedule reconstructs the leak in the order it happened.|a schedule is drafted to be comprehensive and its ordering carries no meaning.]]

## Requested, not learned

Waluigi wants to slow down on one word in item iii because the whole exhibit turns on it.

The schedule does not say *the identity of the person who disclosed the route*. It does not say *learned*, *overheard*, or *communicated*. It says **requested**.

A person who discloses a route is a leak. A person who *requests* a route in advance is something else entirely: they approached the party, asked to be told the way, and were told.

That changes the character of the ambush reconstruction filed alongside this exhibit. The four positions were not the product of somebody betraying information they happened to have. They were the product of somebody going and getting it, deliberately, before the fact, from people who had no reason to refuse.

And the party did tell them, because item iii would not need protecting otherwise.

The archive states the finding narrowly: the route did not escape. It was **collected**. [[roll:6|Whoever laid the ambush had a source who could ask the party a direct question and receive a truthful answer|and that is a much smaller category of person than 'someone who found out'. It requires standing, access, and a plausible reason to be asking about a morning's route through a commercial ward.|a request for a route could have come from any porter, guide or hired hand and implies no closeness at all.]].

## Consideration stated as received, amount not entered

The last line of the counterpart is the one Waluigi would take into a court, if this file had a court.

*Consideration stated as received. Amount not entered on the counterpart.*

Silence contracts are paid for. That is what makes them contracts rather than requests. The counterpart records that payment was made and deliberately omits how much, which is a standard device — the paying party keeps the sum on their copy only, so that a leaked counterpart cannot be used to establish the scale of what was being bought.

But the omission is itself informative in combination with item iv, which forbids discussing *any sum paid in connection with items i to iii*.

So there are two payments in this document's world. There is the consideration for the silence, which is on the other copy. And there is whatever was paid in connection with the route, which item iv exists to bury.

The archive holds neither figure and will not guess at them. What it holds is the structure, and the structure is that [[roll:4|somebody was paid for the route and then somebody was paid again to stop the first payment being mentioned|item iv is not protecting the silence money, which is covered by the contract's own nature. It is protecting an earlier transaction, which means the contract is the second purchase in this sequence rather than the first.|item iv is routine drafting to prevent the contract's own consideration being disclosed.]]

exhibits.title: Offering List — Entry Five Is in a Different Hand
exhibits.onRecord: The offering list from the Festival of the Fallen. Grain, salt and oil, one measure each, from the district collectively. Then a name, spoken, from each household in turn. Those four are in the table clerk's hand, and the list is ruled off beneath them. Below the rule, in another hand, entry five: *an undertaking, given aloud, on behalf of the living.* No giver named. [[roll:4|The rite has no category for an undertaking|grain, salt, oil and names are what this festival has always taken. Somebody made a promise at the offering table that the ceremony had no slot for, and a second person decided afterwards that the record could not be allowed to omit it.|festival clerks add late entries constantly and the second hand is just whoever tidied up.]]
exhibits.analysis:
## A ruled line is a decision

Waluigi would like to explain why a horizontal line matters, because it is the load-bearing feature of this document and it looks like nothing.

A clerk rules off a list when the list is complete. It is a formal act: it closes the record, prevents interpolation, and states that the four entries above are all there were. Every offering table in every rite this archive has records of does the same thing.

So at the moment the rule was drawn, the festival's official position was that four offerings had been made.

Entry five is below it, in a different hand.

That tells us three things in order. The undertaking was given **after** the offerings had been closed. The clerk who closed the list did not record it, either because they did not consider it an offering or because they were not asked to. And somebody else — not the clerk — decided that the omission was unacceptable and corrected the record in a way that cannot be mistaken for the original.

That last point deserves credit. The second hand did not forge the clerk's writing or insert the entry above the rule, both of which would have been easy. They wrote it plainly, below the line, where it is obviously an addition, which means [[roll:5|the amendment was made by somebody who wanted it to be visible as an amendment|a person concealing an interpolation puts it in the body of the list. A person creating a truthful record of an irregularity puts it below the rule in their own hand and lets the reader see exactly what happened.|writing below a ruled line is what anybody does when they run out of space and implies no intention whatsoever.]].

## No giver named

The archive now has to be honest about the limit of this exhibit, because the temptation is to read entry five as a confession and it is not one.

Every other entry has a giver. The district collectively, for the grain, salt and oil. Each household in turn, for the names.

Entry five has none. *An undertaking, given aloud, on behalf of the living.*

That phrasing is careful to the point of being lawyerly, and Waluigi does not think that is accidental. It records that the thing happened. It records that it was audible. It records that it purported to bind a group rather than an individual. And it names nobody at all.

Somebody wanted the fact preserved and the person protected, and those two aims are in tension in every record ever kept.

Read against the Sovereignty Act notice filed later in this session, the protection turns out to be worth much less than the recorder hoped, because clause 5 of the Act catches everybody present who did not dissent aloud. So the anonymity of entry five protects [[roll:6|nobody, once the Act's collective clause is applied|the recorder shielded the speaker's name and the statute does not require a name. 'Given aloud, on behalf of the living' is, on the Act's own wording, an admission against every person standing in that circle.|leaving the giver blank is precisely what makes the entry useless to any prosecutor and the protection worked.]].

## What the district actually gave

Waluigi will finish on the four entries above the line, because the file keeps treating them as scene-setting and they are not.

Grain, salt and oil. One measure each. From the district collectively.

That is a poor district's offering and it is also a district's **entire ceremonial vocabulary** — the three things that keep people alive through a winter, given in the smallest honest quantity. Nobody was showing off.

Then a name from each household. Not a donation. A name, spoken, which costs nothing and is the only offering the festival actually exists for.

And then, below the line, in a hand that is not the clerk's, an undertaking.

The distance between entry four and entry five is the distance between a community remembering its dead and a community pledging its living, and the ceremony had no procedure for the second because no one had ever tried to make it there before.

The archive's finding is not about who spoke. It is that [[roll:4|the rite was used as an instrument, and the record shows the seams|the offering table had categories for goods and for names and was made to accept a third thing it was not built for. That is why the entry is below the line in a different hand. A tradition that had a slot for undertakings would have had a clerk who wrote it in the list.|the festival has always been flexible and reading procedural significance into an informal list is overinterpretation.]]

exhibits.title: Terms Memorandum — A Garrison You Asked For Is a Garrison
exhibits.secured: Contemporaneous memorandum, taken at the circle
exhibits.onRecord: A memorandum taken at the circle while the terms were still being spoken. Asked of the district: that armed men of the Loyalist establishment be quartered within it, permanently, at the district's own request. Offered in return: recognition, standing, the rite completed rather than abandoned. One voice objected — *a garrison you asked for is still a garrison* — and was answered: *a garrison you asked for is a garrison you can un-ask.* [[roll:5|Nobody in the circle raised the Mandate|and the whole exchange depends on whether the un-asking has legal effect, which is a question the Iron Mandate answers and which no one present asked.|a ritual circle is no place for statutory argument and the omission means nothing.]]
exhibits.analysis:
## The best document in this investigation

Waluigi says this without qualification. A contemporaneous memorandum taken by a participant while a negotiation is happening is the rarest and most valuable thing an archive can hold, and it is rarer still to get one that records the objection as well as the terms.

Most accounts of negotiations are written by winners, afterwards, and describe an inevitability. This one was written in the middle, by somebody who did not know how it would end, and it preserves the moment when it could still have gone the other way.

Four clauses. What was asked. What was offered. What was objected. What was answered.

The asking is unambiguous and the memorandum does not soften it: armed men of the Loyalist establishment, quartered within the district, **permanently**, and at the district's own request. Every element of that sentence is a term of art and the fourth is the operative one.

The offering is vaguer, and Waluigi notes the asymmetry with some professional discomfort. Recognition. Standing. The rite completed rather than abandoned. Those are real goods but none of them is measurable, deliverable on a date, or capable of being enforced, whereas [[roll:4|the thing being asked for is specific, permanent and physical|men in buildings. One side of this bargain can be counted and the other cannot, which is the oldest asymmetry in the negotiating trade and the memorandum records it without appearing to notice.|recognition and standing are the most valuable things a marginal community can obtain and dismissing them as vague is the archive's cynicism, not analysis.]].

## The objection was right and the answer was better

The exchange in clauses 3 and 4 is the finest piece of dialogue in this file and Waluigi wants to take it apart properly, because both speakers were intelligent and only one of them was correct.

*A garrison you asked for is still a garrison.* That is true and it is the sort of truth that loses arguments, because it sounds like refusing to engage. The objector is saying that the character of a thing is not changed by the manner of its arrival, which is philosophically sound and rhetorically fatal.

*A garrison you asked for is a garrison you can un-ask.* That is a genuinely excellent reply. It concedes the objection entirely and then relocates the question from character to **control**. Yes, it is a garrison; the difference is that this one has a door you hold.

It is also, and the memorandum's own last clause is what proves it, false.

Clause 7 of the Iron Mandate permits armed men maintained at the request of a recognised authority where the request is recorded. Clause 9 provides that the Legion determines what is a recognised authority.

So the request is the door and the Legion holds the handle. The district cannot un-ask, because the moment it tries, the Legion is entitled to decide the district was never a recognised authority to begin with — at which point the request stands, the men stay, and the withdrawal has no legal existence. [[roll:6|The answer at the circle described a right the district does not have|and it was accepted because it was the more comforting of two accurate-sounding sentences. The objector was right and lost, which is the ordinary fate of people who are right about structure while everyone else is talking about intention.|clause 9 is a formality and no authority genuinely revokes recognition of a community it has just made an agreement with.]]

## The clause that is not there

The memorandum's final line is the archive's favourite kind of entry: an honest record of an absence, written by the person who noticed it.

*Not addressed. Whether the un-asking has any legal effect. Nobody in the circle raised the Mandate.*

Waluigi has thought about why. The Mandate is not obscure — it is an enrolled statute with an extract posted in the ward — and there were people in that circle capable of reading it.

The answer is probably the least sinister available: they were in a rite, at night, at a festival for the dead, being offered recognition by something that had never offered it before, and statutory construction is not what that room was for. The negotiation happened in a register where the binding force of a promise felt self-evident, and the question of what a magistrate would later make of it did not arise.

That is not stupidity. It is a category error, and it is the specific category error this entire investigation is about: a pact made in the language of obligation, landing in a world that runs on the language of licences.

The memorandum-taker deserves the last word, because they saw it at the time and wrote it down anyway. [[roll:4|Recording the question nobody asked is worth more than recording the answers|four clauses of terms are useful and the fifth is decisive, because it is the only evidence the archive has that the omission was an omission rather than a considered decision. Somebody in that circle knew the Mandate existed and did not get the chance to say so.|noting an unaddressed point is standard minute-keeping and implies nothing about anyone's knowledge.]]

exhibits.title: Iron Mandate — Clause Seven Is the Door, Clause Nine the Handle
exhibits.secured: Extract certified against the enrolled text
exhibits.onRecord: Four operative clauses of the Iron Mandate, recitals cut. Clause 2: no body but the Legion may maintain armed men in a ward. Clause 3: consent of the ward does not save you. Clause 7: nothing applies to men maintained at the request of a recognised authority, where the request is recorded. Clause 9: [[roll:4|the Legion determines what is a recognised authority|so the exemption in clause 7 is not a right, it is a permission that the exempting body can withdraw by redefinition. The statute grants a shelter and gives the other side the key to it in the next clause but one.|clause 9 is an ordinary administrative provision and every statute needs somebody to make determinations under it.]]. Penalty on conviction under clause 2: forfeiture of the premises and dispersal of the body.
exhibits.analysis:
## Why the archive cut the recitals

Waluigi has removed roughly nine tenths of the Iron Mandate from this exhibit and should account for it, since cutting a statute is exactly the sort of thing this file criticises other people for.

The omitted material is recitals and schedules: what the Mandate is for, who moved it, what mischief it addresses, and a long list of wards and definitions. All of that is context and none of it changes a single outcome.

The four clauses reproduced here are the ones that do work, and they are reproduced in full and in order, which is the standard this archive holds itself to. A reader who wants the recitals may have them; a reader who wants to know what happens to the district needs these four sentences and nothing else.

Read them as a machine rather than as prose.

Clause 2 prohibits. Clause 3 closes the obvious escape — you cannot consent your way out. Clause 7 opens a different escape, conditioned on a **request** by a **recognised authority**, **recorded**. Clause 9 places the definition of one of those three conditions entirely in the hands of the prohibiting party.

That is a well-built machine and Waluigi admires it in the way one admires a good trap. [[roll:5|Clause 3 exists to force everybody through clause 7|without it, a district could simply agree to host men and the question of recognition would never arise. Clause 3 removes the cheap route so that the only lawful arrangement is one that runs through a definition the Legion controls.|clause 3 is an anti-avoidance provision of the most routine kind and reading strategy into it is fanciful.]]

## Recognised authority

The phrase is doing more damage than any other three words in this investigation, and the damage is invisible until you ask what the district's status actually is.

A recognised authority, on the Mandate's own terms, is whatever the Legion says it is. There is no register, no test, no appeal, and no requirement that a determination be made in advance or communicated at all.

That produces a peculiar and quite deliberate condition: the district cannot know, at the moment it makes the request, whether the request is worth anything. It only finds out later, and only if the question is litigated, and the answer at that point will be given by the body prosecuting it.

Waluigi wants the practical consequence stated in the plainest available words. The district is currently in one of two states and has no way to determine which. Either it is a recognised authority, its request is valid, the garrison is lawful and it may in principle un-ask — or it is not, the request is a nullity, and the garrison in its streets is an unlawful body maintained in a ward, which under clause 2 makes [[roll:6|the district itself liable to the penalty, not the garrison|forfeiture of the premises and dispersal of the body. If the request is void, the men are being maintained by a body other than the Legion in a ward, and the premises forfeited are the district's own. The trap is not that they might lose the garrison. It is that they might lose the buildings.|the penalty would fall on whoever maintains the men, which is the Loyalist establishment, not the district that requested them.]].

## The clause nobody has used

There is one word in clause 7 the archive has not yet exploited and it is the only piece of good news in this exhibit.

*Where the request is recorded.*

Recorded is a documentary requirement and documentary requirements are the one thing this archive is genuinely equipped to fight about. It means there must be a record. A record has a form, a date, a custodian and a text, and any of those can be defective.

The quartering return filed later in this session shows six premises taken and three of them held with no men in them, which is a use of the request that the request may well not cover. The terms memorandum shows what was asked at the circle, and what was asked was *quartering*, not the taking of an assembly hall, a granary and a watch house.

So the live question is not the grand constitutional one of recognition, which the district cannot win. It is the narrow one: [[roll:4|does the recorded request match what has actually been taken|because clause 7 exempts only what was requested, and the quartering return lists three buildings that nobody at the circle asked anybody to occupy. That is not sedition, it is a discrepancy between two documents, and discrepancies are winnable.|clause 9 lets the Legion resolve any such discrepancy in its own favour along with everything else.]]

exhibits.title: Public Notice — Clause Five Makes Every Silent Bystander a Seditionist
exhibits.secured: Posted notice, ward office copy stamped and dated
exhibits.onRecord: The Supernatural Sovereignty Act, in the summary posted for the district. No allegiance, undertaking or covenant to any power not of the mortal establishment. An undertaking given in the course of a rite counts. The offence is complete on the giving — performance is not required. It is triable as sedition. And clause 5: [[roll:5|where the undertaking is given collectively, every person present who did not dissent aloud is taken to have given it|which converts attendance into participation. The offering list records an undertaking 'given aloud, on behalf of the living', and clause 5 supplies the missing defendants that the list carefully declined to name.|collective-liability clauses are unenforceable in practice and no court would convict a bystander on one.]]. Posted three streets from the festival ground.
exhibits.analysis:
## The offence is complete on the giving

Waluigi wants to start with clause 3, because it is the clause that removes every defence anybody in this district would instinctively reach for.

*The offence is complete on the giving. Performance is not required.*

The natural argument — nothing happened, no one did anything, it was words at a festival — is foreclosed by a single sentence. The Act does not punish the consequences of a pact. It punishes the pact.

That is not an unusual drafting choice for a sedition statute and Waluigi does not think it is uniquely sinister. Conspiracy offences work the same way everywhere, for the sensible reason that a state that must wait for performance is a state that must wait to be attacked.

What it does mean is that the entire evidential question collapses down to whether an undertaking was given, and the archive is in possession of an offering list, below a ruled line, in a second hand, recording *an undertaking, given aloud, on behalf of the living*.

The recorder who wrote that entry was, Waluigi is fairly confident, trying to be honest about the rite and to protect the speaker by omitting the name. Against clause 3, honesty is the only element the prosecution needs, and [[roll:4|the protective omission of the name does not help, because clause 3 does not require one|the offence is the giving, and the list proves a giving. A prosecutor needs the act, not the actor, to establish that the offence occurred; the actor comes from clause 5.|no tribunal convicts on an anonymous line in a festival list and the entry is worthless as evidence.]]

## Clause five

This is the one that should empty a room and Waluigi is going to be precise about how it works, because vagueness here helps nobody.

Where the undertaking is given collectively, **every person present who did not dissent aloud** is taken to have given it.

Three conditions. The undertaking must be collective — entry five says *on behalf of the living*, which is as collective as language gets. The person must have been present. And they must not have dissented aloud.

The terms memorandum records exactly one voice objecting: *a garrison you asked for is still a garrison.* One.

So on the face of these two documents, the sole person in that circle with a defence under clause 5 is the individual who argued against the pact and lost. Everybody who stood there in agreement, or in doubt, or in silence because they were not sure what was happening, is caught.

Waluigi finds this genuinely ugly and will say so, while conceding that it is not novel; collective-liability provisions appear in emergency legislation throughout this archive's holdings. The distinctive cruelty here is procedural rather than moral. In a rite, at night, at a festival for the dead, **silence is the expected behaviour**. The Act requires people to break a ceremony in order to preserve their innocence, and [[roll:6|the district's own custom is what convicts it|clause 5 is written for meetings, where speaking is normal and silence is assent. Applied to a rite where silence is the form of participation, it makes the observance itself the evidence.|the clause applies identically to any gathering and the ritual context changes nothing in law.]].

## Posted three streets away

The last finding is not about the text at all. It is about where the paper was nailed up and when.

The archive's copy is the ward office's, stamped and dated, and the posting was made in this district, this quarter, three streets from the festival ground.

A public notice is a legal act. Its purpose is to fix knowledge — after posting, nobody may say they did not know. And the choice of where to post is made by an official, from a list of wards, one at a time.

Somebody chose this district, in the quarter of the festival.

Waluigi is not going to claim that proves foreknowledge of the pact, because it does not; the Act is general, postings are routine, and a district hosting a large public rite is an obvious place to post a notice about rites. The innocent reading is entirely available.

But the effect is not innocent, whatever the intention was. The posting means that on the night of the festival, every person in that circle was, in law, on notice of clause 5. And it means that if anybody wanted a prosecution to be easy, [[roll:4|the hard part was already done before the offence occurred|posting fixes knowledge, and knowledge is the element most commonly fatal to sedition charges. Whoever nailed that summary up three streets away removed the district's best defence a fortnight in advance, by doing nothing more sinister than their job.|notice provisions are satisfied by publication anywhere in the city and the choice of district has no legal consequence at all.]]

exhibits.title: Quartering Return — The Three Buildings With Nobody In Them
exhibits.onRecord: The quartering return. Thirty-six men in three places: twenty-four in the old customs shed, twelve in two riverside houses, compensation paid for both. And three further premises taken with no men in them and no compensation, entered as *not occupied* — the district meeting hall, the upper floor of the granary, and the east gatehouse that housed the district watch. [[roll:4|The return defines 'not occupied' as premises to which the garrison holds the key and in which no man sleeps|so the empty buildings are not empty. They are held, and the definition was written down by the people holding them, which is why the archive can state it rather than infer it.|an unoccupied building is unoccupied and the definition is bookkeeping pedantry.]]
exhibits.analysis:
## Count the buildings, not the men

Thirty-six men is the number everybody quotes and Waluigi considers it the least informative figure on the page.

Thirty-six is not an occupation force. It could not hold a district of four hundred households against any determined resistance, and if the question were military, the district would have considerable grounds for confidence.

The question is not military. Look at what was taken.

The meeting hall, which is where the district assembles. The upper floor of the granary, which is where its food is. The east gatehouse, which is where its watch was based.

Those three buildings are the district's capacity to gather, to feed itself, and to police itself, and all three were taken with no men in them and no compensation paid.

The two categories on this return are doing entirely different jobs. The customs shed and the riverside houses are **billets** — thirty-six men have to sleep somewhere, compensation was paid, and this is the ordinary unpleasant business of quartering. The other three are **instruments**. [[roll:5|A garrison that takes the assembly hall, the grain and the watch house has not occupied a district, it has decommissioned one|billets are where soldiers live. Keys to the hall, the granary and the gatehouse are the three levers by which a community organises, survives and defends itself, and holding them requires no men at all.|three unused buildings held by a small garrison are a logistical convenience and reading a doctrine into them is overreach.]].

## Not occupied

The archive is grateful to whichever clerk defined the term, because it saved this exhibit from being an inference.

*Premises to which the garrison holds the key and in which no man sleeps.*

That definition was written by the occupying side, in their own return, for their own purposes — almost certainly to justify paying no compensation, since compensation attaches to occupation and this is carefully not occupation.

In doing so they wrote down the mechanism. The garrison holds the key. The building is not used. Nobody is compensated. And the district cannot assemble in its own hall, draw its own grain, or man its own gatehouse, because the key is elsewhere.

The accounting motive makes it more reliable rather than less. A clerk minimising a compensation liability is not thinking about how the entry will read to an archive two seasons later; he is thinking about the column total. Self-interested documents are the honest ones, which is the same lesson the portage bill taught in the first session.

Waluigi's finding: the return proves control of the three critical buildings **on the occupier's own definition**, and no testimony is required to establish it. [[roll:6|The compensation column is the confession|paying for the billets and refusing to pay for the hall, the granary and the gatehouse concedes that the garrison does not regard the second group as occupied, while the definition concedes they hold the keys. Both admissions are needed and both are on the same page.|the compensation distinction is a routine accounting rule applied identically across every quartering return in the service.]]

## What this does to the petition

The exhibit filed next to this one is the district's petition to rescind the request, and this return explains its arithmetic before anybody reads it.

One hundred and forty-one signatures out of roughly four hundred households. Thirty-eight refusals, of which thirty-one gave the same reason: *the grain is in the granary and the garrison has the key.*

That is not apathy and it is not collaboration. It is thirty-one households performing exactly the analysis this exhibit has just performed, faster and with more at stake, and concluding that a petition is not survivable while somebody else holds the food.

The circulator's note confirms the geography of it. Support was strongest in the riverside streets, where men are billeted in front rooms, and weakest nearest the granary.

Waluigi wants that inversion understood, because it is counter-intuitive and it is the most humane thing in this file. The people with soldiers actually living in their houses were the most willing to sign. The people with no soldiers anywhere near them, but with a key held over their winter stores, were not.

[[roll:4|Proximity to soldiers produces resistance and proximity to the granary produces compliance|which tells you that the garrison's leverage is not fear of violence. Nobody near the billets is frightened of the men. Everybody near the grain is frightened of the key, and the key was obtained without a single threat being made.|both groups are responding to the same intimidation and the difference is simply that riverside households had less to lose.]]

exhibits.title: Petition — Thirty-One Households Gave the Same Reason
exhibits.secured: Petition with circulator's return of refusals
exhibits.onRecord: The district's petition to rescind the request under which the garrison is quartered. One hundred and forty-one signatures from a district of roughly four hundred households. Thirty-eight refused, and thirty-one of those gave a reason so uniform the circulator recorded it once: [[roll:4|"The grain is in the granary and the garrison has the key."|thirty-one households independently arriving at identical words is not thirty-one opinions, it is one fact that everybody near the granary can see. The circulator recorded it once because writing it thirty-one times would have added nothing.|a circulator paraphrasing a general mood into a single quotation is normal practice and the uniformity is his, not theirs.]]. Support strongest riverside, weakest nearest the granary.
exhibits.analysis:
## The refusals are the document

A petition with a hundred and forty-one names on it is a weak instrument and Waluigi is not going to pretend otherwise. Four hundred households, a third signing, no legal effect, addressed to an authority whose recognition is itself in question.

As a political act it will achieve nothing. As a **survey** it is the best data in this investigation, and the reason is the circulator's return of refusals, which is a piece of record-keeping most petitions do not bother with.

Most circulators record only the names they got. This one recorded who said no, how many, and why, which converts an advocacy document into something the archive can actually reason from.

Thirty-eight refused. Thirty-one of them gave the same reason. And the seven others gave reasons the circulator did not record, which Waluigi flags as the one gap in an otherwise disciplined return — seven households declined for reasons nobody now knows, and [[roll:5|the unrecorded seven are the only group in this district whose position is genuinely unknown|the signers signed, the thirty-one explained themselves, and the unasked were never approached. Seven households looked a circulator in the face, refused, and gave a reason he chose not to write down.|seven unrecorded refusals out of four hundred households is statistical noise and means nothing.]].

## One sentence, thirty-one times

The archive wants to defend the reliability of the quoted reason, because a single recorded quotation attributed to thirty-one households is exactly the sort of thing a careful reader should distrust.

The defence is the geography. The circulator's note says support was strongest in the riverside streets and weakest nearest the granary, and that gradient is independent of the quotation — it comes from the signature sheet itself, which is organised by street.

So there are two separate pieces of evidence pointing the same way. The words the refusers used, which come from the circulator and could in principle be his summary. And the distribution of signatures across the district, which comes from the sheet and cannot be summarised by anybody.

The distribution confirms the words. Whatever the thirty-one actually said, their behaviour was determined by distance from the granary, which is precisely what the quotation describes.

Waluigi therefore treats the sentence as reliable in substance if not in exact wording, and notes the methodological point for future files: [[roll:6|a quotation is corroborated when an independent variable in the same document behaves as the quotation predicts|the circulator could have invented the sentence. He could not have invented the street-by-street signature pattern, and the two agree. That is corroboration from inside a single document, which is rare and worth naming.|a circulator who would invent a quotation would happily arrange the signature sheet to match it.]].

## What the district actually asked for

The prayer of the petition deserves attention because it is narrower than the mood around it, and the narrowness is deliberate.

*That the request under which armed men are quartered in this district be rescinded, and the premises returned.*

Not that the garrison be expelled. Not that the pact be repudiated. Not a word about the festival, the undertaking, or anything that would engage the Sovereignty Act.

Whoever drafted this understood the legal position rather well. Attacking the pact means admitting the pact, and clause 5 of the Act would then convict everybody who signed. Attacking the **request** engages the Iron Mandate instead, where the district's argument is at least arguable, and where the quartering return provides the concrete grievance — three premises taken that nobody at the circle asked for.

So the petition is not a cry of protest. It is a carefully bounded legal move by somebody who has read both statutes and picked the only fight available.

That person is not named anywhere on the document, and Waluigi thinks that is also deliberate. The archive's assessment is that this petition was drafted competently, aimed correctly, and will still fail — because [[roll:4|it asks the recognised authority to rescind, and clause 9 lets the Legion decide there is no recognised authority to do the rescinding|the petition's own addressee is the weak point. It is drafted around the Mandate and defeated by the same statute one clause later, which is a trap no amount of good drafting escapes from inside the district.|a rescission petition to the requesting authority is procedurally correct and the Legion's determination power is irrelevant to it.]]

exhibits.title: Patrol Book — The Patrols Went Down, Not Up
exhibits.secured: Legion patrol book, ward extract, twelve weeks
exhibits.onRecord: Twelve weeks of the Legion patrol book. Trade Ward patrols hold steady at twenty-one or twenty-two every single week. District patrols run at eighteen to twenty for four weeks, decline through the middle of the period, and reach zero by week twelve. The standing instruction entered in week nine reads: [[roll:4|"District policed by arrangement. Patrols not required."|the Legion did not increase its presence after the pact. It stopped coming, and wrote down that it had stopped because an arrangement now did the work. Withdrawal, not reinforcement, is what the agreement produced.|a fall in patrols in one district over twelve weeks is ordinary redeployment and the note is routine.]]
exhibits.analysis:
## The control group is on the same page

Waluigi is fond of this document for a reason that has nothing to do with the district: it contains its own control.

A declining series on its own proves very little. Patrols fall for a dozen reasons — manpower, weather, a quiet season, an inspection elsewhere — and any of them would explain eighteen becoming zero.

But the Trade Ward column is on the same page, kept by the same book, over the same twelve weeks, and it does not move. Twenty-one, twenty, twenty-two, twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-one, twenty-three, twenty-two, twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-one, twenty-two.

That is a flat line. Whatever pressures the Legion was under during this period, they did not affect the ward next door.

So the decline is specific to the district and cannot be attributed to general redeployment, which is the explanation anybody would reach for first. [[roll:5|The two columns together turn a trend into a decision|one falling series is a circumstance. A falling series beside a flat one, in the same book, over the same weeks, is a choice made about one district and not the other.|the two areas have different requirements and comparing their patrol counts is not meaningful.]]

## Week nine

The standing instruction is dated and that date is the finding.

The decline does not begin in week nine — it begins around week six and is well advanced by week eight, falling from nineteen to nine. Week nine is when somebody wrote it down.

That ordering matters. An instruction that *caused* a change appears before the change. An instruction that appears in the middle of a change is **ratifying** it: an officer noticing that his men have stopped going somewhere and regularising the position in the book.

So the practice preceded the policy by roughly three weeks, and the policy was written to explain a practice already in place.

Waluigi does not read that as sinister so much as characteristic. Institutions record what they are already doing. But it means the archive should stop looking for a decision to withdraw and start asking what changed in week six, which is the point at which patrols in a district the Legion had policed for years began to become unnecessary.

The quartering return supplies a candidate and the archive offers it as exactly that. [[roll:6|You do not patrol a street whose gatehouse key is in your pocket|the district watch was based in the east gatehouse and the garrison took it. From the moment the keys changed hands the Legion had a policing presence in the district that cost it nothing, and the patrol book records the saving.|the garrison and the Legion are different bodies and one does not substitute for the other in any patrol return.]]

## Policed by arrangement

The archive will finish on the phrase itself, because it is the mildest sentence in this investigation and possibly the worst.

*District policed by arrangement.*

Every word of it is true and none of it is neutral. There is an arrangement — the request, the quartering, the keys. The district is policed. Patrols are, genuinely, not required.

And what the sentence describes is a district that has passed out of the ordinary machinery of the city. Legion patrols are many things, most of them unwelcome, but they are also the mechanism by which a ward is part of the same system as every other ward: the same book, the same rota, the same officers who can be complained to.

A district policed by arrangement has none of that. It has whatever the arrangement provides, administered by a body holding its granary, and no line in the patrol book that anybody outside can inspect.

Waluigi's closing finding for this investigation, and it is the one the whole file has been assembling toward: the pact at the festival was not the moment the district lost anything. Nothing visible happened that night, and the Act's clause 3 notwithstanding, no one has yet been prosecuted.

What happened is administrative and it is complete. [[roll:4|The district was removed from the patrol book, which is the register of places the city considers its own|zero is not an absence of policing. It is the district's name still printed in the column with nothing written against it, week after week, in a book the ward next door appears in twenty-two times. Somebody would have to write a new instruction to bring it back.|a district can be restored to the patrol rota by a single order and the zeros carry no permanence.]]
